title: Two ways to take off $1,000
hook: A $1,000 deduction and a $1,000 credit sound alike. Do they save the same?

knows: that a flat tax rate takes a fixed share of income
doesNotKnow: that a deduction lowers the income the tax is taken from, while a credit lowers the tax bill itself

misconception: A $1,000 deduction and a $1,000 credit are worth the same.
objective: The learner can compute that at a 20% rate a $1,000 deduction cuts the bill by $200 and a $1,000 credit by $1,000, and that a higher rate makes the deduction worth more.

claims.text: On $10,000 of income at a 20% rate the tax is $2,000; a $1,000 deduction leaves $9,000 to be taxed, so the tax is $1,800, a cut of $200 (20% of $1,000).
A $1,000 credit makes the same $2,000 bill $1,000, a cut of $1,000.

A deduction is worth the tax rate times its size (so more at higher rates); a credit is worth its full size at any rate (when the bill is at least as large). The stage lets the learner raise the rate with both shown.
claims.source: At 10%, 20%, 40% the deduction cuts 100, 200, 400 and the credit 1,000 (node; Demo.tsx dedBill(), credBill()).

claims.text: A deduction subtracts from the income the tax is taken from; a credit subtracts from the tax bill itself.
claims.source: Standard definitions of tax deduction and tax credit (general public-finance texts).

claims.text: The lesson uses a fictional tax system with invented numbers and one flat rate; it is not any country's rules and not tax advice.
claims.source: Stage chip 'Made-up system: income $10,000, one flat rate'.

recall.question: In a made-up flat 25% system, which saves more tax: a $400 deduction or a $150 credit?
recall.why: The deduction cuts the bill by 25% of $400 = $100. The credit cuts it by the full $150.
